procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated October 18, 1968 of the Bombay High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 1161 of 1966, allowing the oral application of the respondent's advocate for amendment of the charge and directing a new trial on the amended charge.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The second respondent Bank filed a complaint against the appellant alleging misappropriation. The Magistrate framed a charge under s. 406, Penal Code, for misappropriation of moneys. The appellant was convicted and appealed to the High Court. During the appeal, the High Court allowed an oral application to amend the charge to include misappropriation of goods and directed a new trial on the amended charge, keeping the appeal pending.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the High Court's order, arguing that the order for a new trial was unwarranted, unfair, and unsupported by the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, finding no reason to interfere with the High Court's discretion in framing the charge and giving the accused an opportunity to meet the additional charge.

issue.issue_text: Whether an appellate court can amend a charge when the prosecution did not seek such an amendment during the trial.

facts: During an appeal against a conviction, the prosecution made an oral application to amend the charge to include an alternative charge (misappropriation of goods in addition to misappropriation of money).
The appellant argued that the prosecution should not be allowed to amend the charge at the appellate stage since it had not insisted on this additional charge during the trial.
The High Court allowed the amendment and sent the case back to the trial court to give the appellant a full opportunity to defend against the amended charge.
law: The Code of Criminal Procedure grants ample power to both trial and appellate courts to alter or amend a charge.
Specifically, Section 423(1)(d) of the Code empowers an appellate court to make any amendment or consequential order that is just and proper.
Section 535 of the Code further illustrates this wide power, stating that a conviction is not invalid even if a charge was omitted, unless it caused a failure of justice.
This power is supported by precedent from the Privy Council (Thakar Sahab v. Emperor), which affirmed the wide powers of an appellate court to alter charges.
application: The Supreme Court held that the power to amend a charge at the appellate level is subject to a crucial limitation: the accused must not be prejudiced.
Prejudice would occur if the amendment introduces a completely new offence or if the accused is not given a full opportunity to meet the new charge and present a defense.
In this case, the Court found no prejudice. The amended charge was an alternative under the same section of the Penal Code (s. 406) and arose from the same single, indivisible transaction.

Furthermore, the High Court's order did not direct a full retrial but specifically sent the case back to give the appellant an opportunity to recall witnesses and adduce new evidence, thereby safeguarding against any potential prejudice.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, concluding that an appellate court has the power under the Code of Criminal Procedure to amend a charge, even if not requested at trial, provided that the amendment does not cause prejudice to the accused by introducing a new offence or denying them a full opportunity to present a defense.

issue.issue_text: Whether amending a charge from criminal breach of trust concerning money to an alternative charge concerning goods purchased with that money amounts to a new charge on a new subject matter, thereby causing prejudice to the accused.

facts: The accused was initially charged with criminal breach of trust for misappropriating money advanced to him by a bank under a Packing Credit Agreement.
During the appeal in the High Court, the charge was amended to include an alternative charge of misappropriating the goods that were purchased with that money.
The accused (appellant) argued that this amendment constituted a totally new charge concerning a new subject matter (goods instead of money), which would prejudice his defence.
law: The offence under the Indian Penal Code (s. 406) remained the same for both the original and the alternative charge.
Courts have ample power under the Criminal Procedure Code to alter or amend a charge, provided the accused is not charged with a new offence and is not prejudiced by the amendment.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the entire transaction, from the entrustment of money to the purchase of goods with that money, was "one and indivisible."
Because the transaction was indivisible, the alternative charge concerning the goods was not considered a new subject matter but rather a different facet of the same alleged offence.
The Court explicitly stated that the alternative charge did not require the accused to answer to a "new offence," as both charges fell under the same section of the Penal Code (s. 406).

The Court also found that no prejudice was caused to the accused because the High Court's order provided him with a "full opportunity" to defend against the amended charge, including the right to recall witnesses and adduce new evidence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that the amendment did not amount to a new charge on a new subject matter because the money and the goods were part of a single, indivisible transaction. Furthermore, any potential for prejudice was negated by the opportunity given to the accused to fully meet the amended charge.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court's order to amend a charge is invalid if it does not provide specific reasons for finding a prima facie case justifying the amendment.

facts: The appellant argued that the High Court's order to amend a criminal charge was invalid.
The basis for this argument was that the High Court did not consider or provide specific reasons to show that there was a prima facie case to justify the new, amended charge.
law: The Supreme Court noted the broad and extensive powers of an appellate court under the Code of Criminal Procedure to alter or amend charges.
The primary limitation on this power is that the amendment should not prejudice the accused or charge them with a completely new offense without giving them a full opportunity to defend themselves.
application: The Supreme Court acknowledged that the High Court did not explicitly state its reasons for finding a prima facie case for the amended charge.

However, the Court reasoned that the High Court, being an appellate court, was likely being cautious to avoid giving an impression that it had already formed a particular view on the evidence, which could prejudice the ongoing case.
The Court considered the High Court's action a valid "judicial exercise of discretion."
It also pointed out that the appellant had failed to raise this specific ground in their Special Leave Petition.

Finally, the Court reasoned that if the original charge could be framed based on the complaint's allegations, it was not unreasonable for an appellate court to frame an alternative charge based on the same set of allegations without a detailed re-examination.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that the High Court's order to amend the charge was not invalid simply because it did not provide specific reasons for finding a prima facie case. The Court deferred to the High Court's judicial discretion, suggesting the omission was likely intended to avoid prejudicing the trial.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, upon finding it necessary to amend a charge, should have decided the appeal on the original charge instead of keeping it pending and remitting the case for further proceedings on the amended charge.

facts: The appellant was convicted by a Magistrate on a single charge of misappropriation of money under Section 406 of the Penal Code.
The appellant appealed this conviction to the High Court.

During the appeal hearing, the High Court allowed the prosecution's application to amend the charge to include an alternative charge of misappropriation of goods, which arose from the same transaction.

The High Court then ordered the case to be sent back to the Magistrate for further proceedings on the amended charge, specifically to give the appellant a full opportunity to defend against it (e.g., by recalling witnesses).
Crucially, the High Court did not dispose of the appeal but kept it pending until the further proceedings were completed.

The appellant challenged this order, arguing that the High Court should have first decided the appeal on the original charge of misappropriating money before remitting the case for the amended charge.
law: The Supreme Court identified that the Code of Criminal Procedure grants appellate courts extensive powers to alter or amend a charge (specifically citing Section 423).

This power is subject to the condition that the accused is not prejudiced, meaning they are not charged with a completely new offense, are made aware of the new charge, and are given a full opportunity to meet it.
Section 535 of the Code further reinforces the court's power, stating that a finding is not invalid merely because a charge was not framed, unless it has caused a failure of justice.
application: The Supreme Court first clarified that the High Court's order was not for a "new trial" in the full sense, but rather for limited further proceedings to ensure the appellant was not prejudiced by the amendment. This was to give the appellant an opportunity to recall witnesses and present evidence in his defense against the amended charge.

The Court found that no prejudice was caused to the appellant. The amended charge was an alternative, not a completely new offense. It was under the same section of the Penal Code (406) and arose from the same "one and indivisible" transaction.

The Court held that the High Court's decision to keep the appeal pending while the case was remitted was a proper and desirable course of action. This allows the High Court to receive the completed record and dispose of the appeal on both the original and amended charges at once.

The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was acting well within its wide procedural powers. It was not required to first give a finding on the original charge before allowing proceedings on the amended one. The procedure adopted was deemed just and fair to the appellant.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument. It held that the High Court acted correctly and within its extensive powers under the Criminal Procedure Code. The High Court was not obligated to decide the appeal on the original charge before remitting the case for further proceedings on the amended charge. Keeping the appeal pending was a just and proper procedure to ensure the appellant had a fair opportunity to meet the amended charge without causing prejudice, allowing the entire matter to be decided comprehensively upon the return of the case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an appellate court can amend a charge when the prosecution did not seek such an amendment during the trial.
appellant_arguments: The complainant had the opportunity to ask the Magistrate to frame an alternative charge during the trial but failed to do so.
The original charge was framed after substantial evidence had been recorded and after discussions between the parties, yet the charge concerning goods was deliberately omitted.
respondent_arguments: An oral application was made at the appellate stage to add an alternative charge.
Evidence had already been presented during the trial showing that not only the money but also the goods purchased with it were entrusted to the appellant, which justifies the amendment.

arguments.issue_text: Whether amending a charge from criminal breach of trust concerning money to an alternative charge concerning goods purchased with that money amounts to a new charge on a new subject matter, thereby causing prejudice to the accused.
appellant_arguments: Amending the charge at the appellate stage amounts to framing a totally new charge concerning a new subject matter (entrustment of goods).
Allowing such an amendment would prejudice the accused in his defence.
respondent_arguments: The evidence led at trial already covered the entrustment of goods purchased with the advanced money, so it is not an entirely new subject matter.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court's order to amend a charge is invalid if it does not provide specific reasons for finding a prima facie case justifying the amendment.
appellant_arguments: The High Court should have considered whether a prima facie case existed to justify framing the amended charge and should have provided reasons for its conclusion.
respondent_arguments: The text does not explicitly state the respondent's counter-argument, but their position is implicitly that the amendment was justified by the evidence on record, making explicit reasoning unnecessary for the order's validity.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, upon finding it necessary to amend a charge, should have decided the appeal on the original charge instead of keeping it pending and remitting the case for further proceedings on the amended charge.
appellant_arguments: The appellant contended that the High Court took the view that the first charge (regarding money) could not be sustained and therefore should have decided the appeal on that basis, rather than introducing an amendment.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's application for amendment and the High Court's subsequent order to remit the case for a new trial on the amended charge while keeping the appeal pending implicitly argue that this is the correct procedure to ensure justice is done on all aspects of the allegations.

cases.principle: To support the proposition that an appellate court has wide powers under section 423 of the Criminal Procedure Code to alter a charge, and such alteration does not vitiate a conviction as long as the accused is not prejudiced.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under the Criminal Procedure Code, an appellate court has the power to alter or amend a charge, provided that the accused is not prejudiced, is not made to face a charge for a new offense, and is given a full opportunity to meet the amended charge and present a defense.
obiter: While the history and technicalities of English criminal law might make it difficult to justify a variation of a charge, Indian law is governed solely by the Penal Code and Criminal Procedure Code and is not subject to such limitations.
An appellate court may choose not to give detailed reasons for finding a prima facie case for an amended charge to avoid giving an impression that it has taken a particular view on the evidence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: An appellate court has the discretion to amend a charge to include an alternative charge that arises from the same indivisible transaction and is based on evidence already on record. This action does not cause prejudice to the accused, especially when they are given a full opportunity to recall witnesses and adduce new evidence to meet the amended charge. The procedure of keeping the appeal pending while remitting the case for further proceedings on the amended charge is a proper course to ensure justice.
legal_tests_applied: Whether an amendment to a charge causes, or is likely to cause, prejudice to the accused in their defence.
Whether the framing of an amended charge by an appellate court constitutes a proper judicial exercise of discretion.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's contention that the amendment created a new charge on a new subject matter was rejected because the court found the entire transaction was one and indivisible, covering both the money and the goods purchased with it.

The claim of prejudice was dismissed because the alternative charge was based on the 'self same material that has already been brought on record', and the accused was given a full opportunity to recall witnesses or adduce fresh evidence.

The argument that the High Court's order was invalid for not providing reasons for a prima facie case failed because the ground was not raised in the Special Leave Petition, and the Supreme Court deferred to the High Court's 'judicial exercise of discretion' and its desire to avoid giving a premature impression on the evidence.

The argument that the High Court should have decided the appeal on the original charge was found to be based on a 'misreading of the order of the High. Court,' which had correctly kept the appeal pending to allow the accused to meet the amended charge.

The objection to the appellate court framing an alternative charge was dismissed with the logic: 'If no objection could be taken to the trial Court in framing the original charge it is difficult to see how an objection can be taken at this stage to the framing of ap. alternate charge on the same allegation in the complaint.'
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued that the amendment was justified because the alternative charge concerning goods was intrinsically linked to the original charge concerning the money used to purchase them, as part of a single, indivisible transaction.

The respondent's position was strengthened by the commitment that 'no fresh evidence would be led' and they would rely on the existing record, which countered the appellant's claim of being prejudiced by a new case.

The High Court's procedure, which the respondent supported, of keeping the appeal pending while remitting the case for further proceedings on the amended charge was deemed 'desirable and proper' to give the accused a full opportunity to respond.
policy_considerations: The court's primary concern is to safeguard the accused against prejudice by ensuring they have a 'full opportunity to meet this new case,' including the right to recall witnesses or adduce new evidence.

The court recognized that an appellate court, when amending a charge and remitting a case, may legitimately avoid giving detailed reasons for its finding of a prima facie case to prevent giving 'an impression that it has taken any particular view on the evidence,' thereby not prejudicing further proceedings.

The ruling supports a procedural framework that allows for the correction of charges at the appellate stage to align with the evidence, ensuring that a case is decided on its substantive merits rather than on initial charging inaccuracies.
